candidate_sources.title: Maple Anthracnose : Landscape : Center for Agriculture, Food, and the Environment (CAFE) at UMass Amherst
candidate_sources.snippet: Maple anthracnose is caused by several genera of fungi including Aureobasidium, Discula, and Kabatiella. Symptoms vary: Kabatiella causes newly developing leaves to shrivel and turn black; Discula produces tan to reddish-brown lesions centered on veins. The most important management strategy is sanitation: removing infected fallen leaves. Products labeled for use include copper hydroxide + mancozeb, thiabendazole, mancozeb and propiconazole.

candidate_sources.title: Common Disease Pests of Maple in North Carolina | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Dark-colored, irregularly-shaped, angular spots or blotches occur primarily along the midrib, primary veins and leaf margins. Maple anthracnose is caused by Aureobasidium apocryptum, Discula campestris, Colletotrichum gloeosporioides and other fungal pathogens, which overwinter on infected fallen leaves and in twigs and buds. Primarily an aesthetic concern; in severe cases, defoliation and twig dieback can occur.

candidate_sources.title: Maple (Acer spp.)-Anthracnose | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Anthracnose of maple is caused by fungi favored by warm, wet springs. Necrotic spots associated with major leaf veins are characteristic. Management includes sanitation, avoiding overhead irrigation, spacing trees, and fungicide applications beginning at or just before bud break to protect new growth from spring infection.

candidate_sources.title: Anthracnose of shade trees | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Anthracnose is a fungal disease affecting shade trees including maple. Dark brown lesions develop along leaf veins and margins, appearing in spring and expanding into summer. Pathogens overwinter on fallen leaves and twigs. Sanitation by removing infected fallen leaves is the key management strategy.

candidate_sources.title: Eutypella canker | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Eutypella canker is caused by the fungus Eutypella parasitica. A large roughened area of bark, sunken in the center with heavy callus around the margin, is observed on the branch or main trunk. If the bark is peeled back at the center of the canker, a mat of white mycelium will be revealed. Cankers often form on the main trunk or major branches within 9 feet of the ground. Management includes proper pruning cuts, avoiding wounds, mulching, and removing infected branches or trees.

candidate_sources.title: Eutypella Canker On Maple | Penn State Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Eutypella canker is caused by the fungus Eutypella parasitica. The fungus infects recently wounded or newly pruned small branches. A large roughened area of bark, sunken in the center with heavy callus around the margin, is observed on the branch or main trunk. Black fungal fruiting structures protrude from the bark near the centers of older cankers.

candidate_sources.title: Maple Diseases | Penn State Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Overview of maple diseases including Nectria canker, caused by Neonectria galligena and Neonectria cinnabarina, especially common in red and sugar maples, producing dark and wet areas on branches and twigs; cankers grow when the host is stressed. Also covers Eutypella canker and other maple disorders with symptoms, pathogens, and management.

candidate_sources.title: Maple - Steganosporium Canker | University of Maine Cooperative Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Steganosporium canker of maple, a dieback and canker disease of stressed maple trees. Provides plant disease diagnostic images and description of canker symptoms on maple branches and trunks caused by Steganosporium (Stegonsporium) species.

candidate_sources.title: Tar Spot of Maple : Landscape : Center for Agriculture, Food, and the Environment (CAFE) at UMass Amherst
candidate_sources.snippet: Tar spot of maple in northeastern North America is caused by three species of the fungus Rhytisma: R. acerinum, R. punctatum and R. americanum. Early symptoms develop on leaves in early summer as light green to yellow-green spots that deepen and develop small black flecks, enlarging to approximately 3/4 inch. The disease is cosmetic and rarely causes serious defoliation. Management: collect and dispose of fallen leaves by burning, burying, or hot composting.

candidate_sources.title: Tar Spot of Trees and Shrubs â€“ Wisconsin Horticulture
candidate_sources.snippet: Tar spot is a fungal disease caused by species of Rhytisma. Rhytisma americanum infects native maples including sugar, silver, and red maples; Rhytisma acerinum is associated with Norway maple. Initial symptoms are small (~1/8 inch) yellowish spots that enlarge to ~3/4 inch with raised black tar-like structures. The disease is cosmetic and does not kill trees. Management focuses on raking and destroying fallen leaves; fungicides are rarely warranted.

candidate_sources.title: Tar Spots | Diseases of Forest and Shade Trees - University of Minnesota
candidate_sources.snippet: Tar spots on maple are caused by fungi in the genus Rhytisma. On silver maple the black structures are often single, large (~3/4 inch) and raised with convoluted fingerprint-like line patterns. Spots begin as light green or yellow areas in early summer before black stromata develop. The disease is a cosmetic problem and management consists of removing and destroying infected fallen leaves.

candidate_sources.title: Tar spot of maple | Rhytisma spp. | The Morton Arboretum
candidate_sources.snippet: Tar spot of maple is caused by fungi in the genus Rhytisma. Yellow spots appear on leaves in early summer and develop into raised, black, tar-like spots by late summer. The disease is primarily cosmetic and does not significantly harm tree health. Sanitation by raking and disposing of fallen leaves reduces overwintering inoculum.
